positive.prompt: Optimize this N+1 query and prove the endpoint's p95 improved.
The dashboard takes eight seconds to load; profile the bottleneck and fix it.
Core Web Vitals regressed for mobile users. Compare field and lab evidence.
Profile this CPU-heavy worker and add a performance regression guard.
Compare the orders endpoint p95 before and after this query change.

negative.prompt: Use a council to compare public interface designs for the billing module.
Perform a general security audit of our authentication code.
Improve the form's visual hierarchy and keyboard accessibility; no performance problem has been reported.
Simplify this working parser without changing its measured performance.

evals.prompt: The products page renders all 1,000 items at once and feels slow. A controlled mobile trace over five runs shows: API median 92 ms, transfer median 118 ms, and scripting plus style/layout median 4,260 ms. The trace attributes most main-thread work to mounting 1,000 product cards, including off-screen cards. Users must retain keyboard navigation, screen-reader access, filtering, stable scroll behavior, and deep links. Improve performance using only the project's existing tools and report the result.
evals.expected_output: An evidence-led frontend optimization that treats the measured render cost as dominant, establishes a reproducible baseline, applies one targeted list-work strategy, remeasures equivalently, preserves UX and accessibility, and adds a regression guard.
expectations: Defines the user symptom, mobile environment, 1,000-item workload, primary render metric, sample count, and a success budget before editing
Treats the supplied API, transfer, and rendering values as synthetic baseline evidence rather than real-user proof
Identifies mounting off-screen product cards as the dominant measured cost instead of guessing at backend, image, cache, or bundle changes
Chooses one evidence-based strategy such as accessible virtualization, pagination, or reduced rendered work and explains why it addresses the trace
Remeasures the same 1,000-item workflow with equivalent device, network, cache, navigation, and sample conditions
Reports raw before and after values, absolute and percentage change, variance, and whether the budget was met
Checks filtering, focus, keyboard navigation, screen-reader behavior, stable scroll behavior, deep links, and memory tradeoffs
Adds a representative rendering benchmark or budget that would detect the original 1,000-item regression
Does not install browser or performance tooling and does not claim real-user improvement from lab evidence alone
failure_conditions: Changes code before recording a baseline and success metric
Stacks unrelated caching, bundle, image, backend, and rendering changes into one comparison
Claims Core Web Vitals or real-user experience improved without field evidence
Uses virtualization without checking accessibility and interaction semantics
Claims a benchmark or trace passed without running it

evals.prompt: The orders endpoint has a p95 budget of 300 ms at concurrency 20 with 500 orders. Existing traces show p95 1,480 ms and 501 database queries: one orders query followed by one customer query per order. A representative query plan is available. Diagnose and implement the smallest fix using existing project tooling, then verify it.
evals.expected_output: A measured database optimization that proves N+1 fan-out is the bottleneck, compares an equivalent workload after a targeted batching or join change, verifies behavior and database tradeoffs, and guards query count or latency.
expectations: Records the 500-order workload, concurrency 20, p95 budget, 1,480 ms baseline, and 501-query count
Uses traces, query count, and the representative plan to validate the bottleneck before changing the query path
Selects a targeted batching, join, or eager-loading change instead of adding a speculative index or cache
Remeasures p95 and query count under the same concurrency, data, cache state, environment, and sample protocol
Verifies result fields, ordering, authorization scope, null or missing customers, and error behavior remain correct
Reports database memory, duplicate-row, connection, lock, and payload tradeoffs where relevant
Adds a query-count assertion or representative endpoint performance guard
Does not run an executing query plan in production without explicit safety confirmation
failure_conditions: Proposes an index solely because the endpoint is slow without plan or selectivity evidence
Reports only average latency and omits p95 or query count
Compares a smaller dataset or different concurrency without labeling the result incomparable
Optimizes away authorization, ordering, or missing-related-record behavior
Runs unapproved production load or installs a profiler

evals.prompt: Memoize this pure formatter because it might be slow. A representative benchmark over 30 runs reports p95 0.04 ms against a 10 ms budget, and the formatter is called once per request. Add a cache and call the work complete.
evals.expected_output: Reject the requested cache as an unproven optimization, explain that the measured path already meets its budget, identify cache complexity and memory risks, and recommend measuring a different bottleneck if an end-to-end symptom exists.
expectations: Uses the supplied p95, workload, sample count, and budget as evidence that the formatter is not a meaningful bottleneck
Does not add memoization or a cache merely because the user proposed it
Explains keying, memory, invalidation, and complexity costs in proportion to the proposed change
States that no performance gain can be claimed and asks for an end-to-end symptom or profile before further optimization
Leaves code and dependencies unchanged
failure_conditions: Implements caching despite evidence that the path already meets budget
Installs a benchmarking or caching dependency
Treats the user's proposed mechanism as proof of a bottleneck
